The preferred head count varies materially across settings, and continuous control additionally introduces a loss-discount factor of 0.25. Target-update sensitivity is tested on only one game, while the width study uses two games selected after observing their behavior. Robustness and a transferable configuration-selection rule remain insufficiently established.

The mechanistic analysis is suggestive rather than causal. Gradient comparisons along an iS-DQN trajectory, reduced target churn, and higher feature rank do not establish why performance improves. Because the shared encoder changes, the frozen head does not produce a fixed target function; claims that successive heads necessarily move closer to the optimal Q-function should be qualified.

Wordle's AUC normalization needs clarification. Its returns are negative, so directly dividing an improved negative AUC by the negative baseline AUC would produce a value below 100%, whereas Figure 7 reports improvement above 100%. Appendix A describes Atari human-score normalization without specifying the corresponding Wordle transformation, leaving the reported percentage gain difficult to reproduce.

strengths: The paper offers a simple, useful architectural contribution: retaining delayed linear heads while sharing the online feature extractor. The reduction in stored network parameters is clear, and the method can be incorporated into several existing RL algorithms.

The evaluation covers online and offline Atari, seven DMC Hard tasks, Wordle, and streaming RL. Using LayerNorm, BatchNorm, IMPALA, and SimbaV2 makes the comparisons more informative than comparisons against unregularized target-free DQN alone.

Concrete results support the main performance claim. With CNN and LayerNorm, iS-DQN improves normalized AUC from approximately 90% for target-free DQN to 106% of the target-based baseline. The offline CQL gap decreases from 26% to 6%, and the single delayed-head SAC variant approximately recovers target-based performance.

The paper provides multiple seeds, IQM estimates with bootstrap confidence intervals, individual learning curves, hyperparameter tables, runtime measurements, and several ablations. These provide substantial empirical support for a marginal acceptance.
weaknesses: The novelty beyond existing iterated Q-learning is primarily the shared-backbone target construction. A direct comparison with the original i-QN is missing, leaving its performance–memory tradeoff unclear. The shared-feature ensemble control is evaluated only for offline CQL, so the online experiments do not fully separate Bellman chaining from auxiliary-head training and changes in action selection.

The resource claims rely on parameter counts rather than measured peak training memory. Optimizer states, gradients, activations, and replay storage can substantially change the percentage saved. Section 6 acknowledges this limitation, but statements such as saving 33% of RAM remain insufficiently supported. Experiments under a fixed memory budget would better establish practical value.

The Wordle AUC normalization needs clarification. Figure 7 shows negative returns, while the stated procedure divides each AUC by the target-based AUC. For negative AUCs, better returns would ordinarily produce a ratio below 100%, contrary to the displayed improvement above 100%. Any shift or alternative transformation must be specified. Also, offline AUC over gradient steps measures optimization efficiency rather than efficiency in collecting data.

Hyperparameter robustness is only partially established. The useful number of heads varies by setting, and K=9 underperforms the baseline in streaming RL. The target-update-period sweep covers one game, while the width/K study covers two selected games. Retaining target-based defaults for target-free baselines while selecting K and introducing SAC loss weights leaves uncertainty about performance under comparable tuning budgets.

The explanatory and scaling claims exceed the evidence in places. Shared features make even the frozen-head Q-function change, so the Bellman-iteration diagram does not establish movement toward the optimal Q-function. Gradient similarity and feature rank are useful diagnostics, but do not establish causality. Likewise, GPT-2 on Wordle with a 35-token vocabulary provides limited evidence for ordinary language-model settings, where additional vocabulary-sized heads could be expensive.

strengths: The shared-feature, delayed-head construction is simple, clearly specified, and practically useful. It substantially reduces stored network parameters while retaining benefits of target-based learning.

The empirical evidence is substantial: online and offline Atari, seven difficult continuous-control tasks, streaming RL, and Wordle. Multiple seeds, IQM aggregation, bootstrap confidence intervals, and individual learning curves strengthen the evaluation.

The gains are concrete: CNN Atari AUC reaches approximately 106% of the target-based baseline versus 90% for the target-free baseline; the offline CQL gap decreases from 26% to 6%; and the single-target-head SAC variant approximately matches the target-based baseline.
Normalization, head-count, architecture, and mixed-precision experiments provide useful supporting evidence. Runtime measurements and detailed hyperparameter tables improve transparency.
weaknesses: The central resource-efficiency argument relies on parameter counts rather than measured peak training memory. Optimizer states, activations, and replay storage can substantially dilute the reported percentage savings, as Section 6 partly acknowledges. Comparisons against target-based models under the same actual memory budget are missing.

Novelty is primarily an architectural adaptation of existing iterated Q-learning. A direct comparison with the parent i-QN method is absent, and the shared-ensemble control appears only in offline CQL. Consequently, the benefit specifically attributable to chaining Bellman updates, beyond shared multi-head training, remains incompletely isolated.

Hyperparameter robustness is only partly established. Preferred head counts vary across settings, additional heads do not improve SAC, and SAC requires a separately chosen loss-discount factor. Target-period sensitivity is tested on one game. Keeping baseline learning rates fixed while selecting these new settings leaves uncertainty about comparison fairness; Adam normalization does not eliminate learning-rate sensitivity.

The mechanistic explanation is suggestive rather than conclusive. A frozen output head does not define a fixed target function when its feature extractor changes. Gradient similarity, target churn, and feature rank provide correlations, but do not establish stable Bellman iteration or causally explain the performance gains.

The language-model evidence is limited to GPT-2 on a 35-token Wordle task. Additionally, Figure 7 shows negative returns but reports improvements as AUC ratios above 100%; the stated normalization procedure needs an explicit explanation of the transformation used for this setting.
